content: 1. Children with congenital heart diseases (CHD) are at an increased risk of contracting COVID-19 and may experience worse outcomes and complications compared to the general pediatric population. This heightened vulnerability is due to their already compromised physiological states and the presence of other co-morbidities associated with CHD. For these individuals, primary prevention measures and strict infection control protocols are of paramount importance. 2. While most children infected with COVID-19 have favorable outcomes, those who require hospitalization are predominantly infants under the age of one and children with underlying medical conditions. 3. Kawasaki disease, also referred to as lymph node syndrome, mucocutaneous node disease, infantile polyarteritis, or Kawasaki syndrome, is a self-limiting vasculitis that affects multiple organ systems, including the skin, mucous membranes, lymph nodes, blood vessel walls, and the heart. Since the emergence of COVID-19, there has been an observed increase in new or concurrent cases of Kawasaki disease in patients testing positive for COVID-19. Although a definitive link between Kawasaki disease and COVID-19 has not yet been established, ongoing research and investigations are being conducted to better understand this potential association. 4. Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) is a severe condition characterized by fever lasting 24 hours or more, laboratory evidence of inflammation (e.g., elevated C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fibrinogen, procalcitonin, D-dimer, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, interleukin-6, elevated neutrophils, reduced lymphocytes, and low albumin), and clinically significant illness requiring hospitalization with involvement of more than two organ systems (e.g., cardiac, renal, respiratory, hematologic, gastrointestinal, dermatologic, or neurological). The diagnosis also requires the absence of alternative plausible explanations and evidence of current or recent SARS-CoV-2 infection or exposure to a confirmed or suspected COVID-19 case within four weeks prior to symptom onset. Although fatalities in hospitalized MIS-C patients are rare, the best preventive measure is to avoid COVID-19 infection through established social distancing and sanitation guidelines. 5. Routine vaccinations, including those for Hepatitis A and B, should continue to be administered to children and adolescents during the COVID-19 pandemic. At every patient visit, healthcare providers should assess the vaccination status of children and adolescents. Unless there are specific contraindications, all due and overdue immunizations should be administered during the visit. According to the CDC, routine vaccinations are an essential preventive care service and should not be delayed due to the pandemic. 6. Vaccinations for infants exposed to Hepatitis B virus (HBV) should not be delayed, even during the COVID-19 pandemic. Timely administration of these vaccines is critical to prevent HBV infection in this vulnerable population.
